title: Epochal Batch Controller — ablation & tuning notes
content:
Purpose:
This doc captures iterative experiments for a new 'epochal' batch controller (controller that groups requests into short-lived epochs/windows and makes epoch-level decisions rather than pure per-request). Goal: reduce p99/p999 tail for mixed-traffic workloads without regressing median latency or throughput. These are ablation-style runs to understand which components matter (epoch boundary flush policy, adaptive timeout, age-normalization fairness, slab assignment).

Quick summary of findings so far (most surprising):
- Age-normalization (scaling urgency by historical arrival rate per key) reduces p99 by ~14% in tails for skewed traffic; small throughput impact (~1–2% GPU utilization) but lower variance across shards.
- Epoch-boundary flush on soft-deadline (flush at epoch end if any request has wait > x) helps p999 more than p99; good for microbursty patterns.
- Disabling the 'slot-stealing' optimization (lets small urgent requests steal slots from queued large batches) reduces fairness problems but increases median by ~6ms under high load.
- Size-adaptive timeouts (timeout proportional to current slot occupancy) reduces average cost per token slightly but can cause starvation for oldest requests if not coupled with age-bump.

Test harness and workload synthesis:
- Workload mixes: 60% embedding short (len 16, tokens), 30% chat turns (len 64), 10% long generation (len 512). Arrival patterns: Poisson baseline, microburst (200–400 req/s bursts every 15s), and heavy-skew (top 5% keys generate 60% of traffic).
- Hardware: rtx-a6000-equivalent hosts, 8k batch mem cap, KV-cache warm for 70% of chat requests.
- Runner: local replay harness: scripts/bench/replay_epochal.sh --seed=4231 --pattern=microburst --scale=1.0 --trace-prefix=epc-
- Metric extraction: perf/collector exports per-trace latency, queue-time, batch-size, epoch-id, slot-id. Aggregation uses internal tool: /tools/latency-agg --buckets p50,p90,p95,p99,p999

Ablation matrix (runs):
1) baseline-epochal: epoch_len=50ms, flush_policy=soft_deadline(100ms), age_norm=on, slot_steal=on
2) no-age-norm: same but age_norm=off
3) hard-flush: flush_policy=epoch_boundary_immediate (no soft deadline)
4) no-slot-steal: slot_steal=off
5) adaptive-timeout-only: age_norm=off, adaptive_timeout=on (timeout=size*(1/(slot_capacity)))
6) full-off: epochal disabled -> falls back to legacy continuous coalescer (for control)

Representative run results (microburst, scale=1.0):
- baseline-epochal: p50=8.6ms, p90=21.3ms, p99=83.4ms, p999=238ms, tokens/s=42.2k, gpu_util=72%
- no-age-norm: p50=8.4ms, p90=20.7ms, p99=96.8ms, p999=312ms, tokens/s=43.0k, gpu_util=73%
- hard-flush: p50=9.1ms, p90=22.5ms, p99=78.2ms, p999=189ms, tokens/s=41.8k, gpu_util=69%
- no-slot-steal: p50=14.7ms, p90=26.8ms, p99=88.1ms, p999=264ms, tokens/s=39.1k, gpu_util=70%
- adaptive-timeout-only: p50=8.2ms, p90=21.0ms, p99=110.5ms, p999=410ms, tokens/s=44.5k, gpu_util=76%
- full-off: p50=10.6ms, p90=28.2ms, p99=142.0ms, p999=610ms, tokens/s=40.0k, gpu_util=66%

Interpretation notes:
- Age-normalization is high signal. Turning it off improves tokens/s slightly but drastically worsens p99/p999. Hypothesis: high-frequency keys dominate slots and starve occasional slow requests; scaling urgency lets rarer keys surface earlier.
- Hard epoch boundary flush improves extreme tail (p999) by ensuring no request waits arbitrarily long across epoch boundaries. However it slightly impacts median/throughput because boundaries sometimes break near-full batches. There's a tunable sweet spot for epoch_len.
- Slot-steal is a latency/throughput tradeoff; it helps tokens/s (and median) but harms worst-case fairness. For multi-tenant SLAs, we should only enable with strict age-bump protections.
- Adaptive timeout without fairness control can be gamed by fast-arriving small requests, leading to starvation and massive p999 regressions in skewed workloads. Always pair adaptive timeout with age-bump or per-key slotted minimums.

Profiling traces & bottleneck signals:
- Traces show most waiting happens in 'epoch_latch.wait' and 'flush_coordinator' events. When p999 spikes, there's also a correlated increase in kernel-queue stalls on the host (~120–180ms idle windows). Not CPU; appears backpressure from slow GPU-side kernel warmups for long requests.
- KV-cache misses amplify tail: requests that miss KV incur extra mem-copy and increase batch processing time variance. Age-normalization decreased the fraction of long-tail KV-miss requests sitting in tail.

Small experiments to try next (prioritized):
- Experiment A: epoch_len sweep: [20ms, 35ms, 50ms, 75ms, 100ms] + soft_deadline=min(2*epoch_len, 120ms). Measure p95/p99/p999 and tokens/s under microburst.
- Experiment B: age-bump policy: when request age > 1.5x median wait, amplify urgency by 2x. Evaluate if this reduces p999 without harming median.
- Experiment C: hybrid slot-steal policy: allow slot stealing only if victim batch size > threshold (e.g., > 32 tokens) and victim age < victim_age_cutoff. Try thresholds 32/64/128.
- Experiment D: KV-cache warmness gating — prefer batching requests with cache hits in same epoch without starving misses (cohort gating).

Operational notes & runs to reproduce:
- Use bench/recipes/microburst_epochal.yaml as input to the runner. Important flags: --trace=true --collect-profile=true --epoch-controller=epochal_v2 --age-norm=true
- Seed traces saved under s3://redwood-prod-bench/epochal/epc-20241102-*/
- Repro command example: ./bench/run_local.sh --config bench/recipes/microburst_epochal.yaml --runs=120 --tag=epc-a01 --seed=4231

Open questions / unknowns:
- How does epochal design interact with model compilation jitter (jit cache miss) at cold starts? We saw one run where p999 blew up due to a reference kernel compile that happened during epoch flush. Need isolation tests.
- Should epoch boundaries align with GPU scheduling slices? Aligning could reduce kernel queue stalls but requires tighter integration with scheduler layer.
- Long-term: can we learn epoch_len and flush thresholds online per-queue using Bayesian optimisation? Concern: unstable configs could oscillate and cause thrashing.

Action items (owners):
- Samir: run epoch_len sweep (Experiment A) at 2 scales (1.0 & 1.6) and upload traces to s3 by EOD next Tue.
- Lucia: prototype age-bump policy in controller/ablation branch (PR link in linked_artifacts) and add unit tests for urgency scaling.
- Noah: instrument kernel-queue metrics in perf agent and correlate with flush events; short PoC to detect compile spikes.
- Maya (me): consolidate sweep results into a Confluence page and sketch a rollout plan for hybrid slot-steal policy.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Might be useful to add 'epoch tombstone' — tiny no-op batch at epoch boundary to force flush but avoid breaking near-full batches (only if backlog < threshold).
- Consider an adaptive age floor per-key (min_age) that prevents tiny keys from being permanently deprioritized in skew.
- For customer-facing SLAs, consider exposing a "fairness mode" toggle that enforces age bumps and disables slot-steal by default.

Long-form appendix (raw trace snippets):
- trace epc-4231-014: long request id r-98765 waited 312ms in queue; at t=300ms event flush_coordinator:forced; batch_size=6 -> processing_time=58ms; result: p999 contributor; KV-miss=true
- trace epc-4231-022: microburst window start +120ms: epoch boundary aligned with burst; hard-flush avoided a >400ms stall for small chat requests.

End of notes. This doc is an evolving notebook — will convert to a proper playbook once we finalize the hybrid policy.
